title: The Periodic Table Is a Map
subtitle: Atoms, elements, and where every one of them came from
subject: Chemistry

pages.h: You are mostly empty space
p: Everything you can touch is made of atoms, and atoms are almost entirely nothing. An atom is about a tenth of a billionth of a metre across. Nearly all of its mass sits in a tiny core called the nucleus, which is tens of thousands of times smaller than the atom itself.

Picture a football stadium. If the stadium is the atom, the nucleus is a pea on the centre spot. Everything else, out to the top row of seats, is the blur of electrons. Electrons are so light and so fast that nobody can say exactly where one is. Physicists describe them as a cloud of probability rather than little balls in orbit.

So why does a table feel solid? Because the electron clouds of the table's atoms push against the electron clouds of your hand's atoms with electric force. You never actually touch anything. You are held a tiny distance away by the same force that makes a balloon stick to a wall. If you could squeeze all the empty space out of every atom in your body, what remained would be smaller than a grain of salt, and it would still weigh as much as you do.
pages.cap: A small, heavy nucleus sits in the middle. A cloud of light, fast electrons fills the rest of the atom.
pages.fact: Did you know? A sheet of paper is about a million atoms thick.

pages.h: Three particles build every element
p: Every atom in the universe is made of just three kinds of particle. Protons carry a positive electric charge. Neutrons carry no charge. Both sit in the nucleus and each weighs about the same. Electrons carry a negative charge, whizz around outside the nucleus, and are tiny: a proton weighs 1,836 times as much as an electron.

Opposite charges attract, so the positive nucleus holds the negative electrons close. But the protons in the nucleus all repel each other. What stops the nucleus from flying apart? A separate force called the strong force, which only works at very short range and glues protons and neutrons together. Neutrons act as spacers that dilute the repelling protons. That is why bigger nuclei need extra neutrons.

An atom with equal numbers of protons and electrons has no overall charge. Take an electron away and you get a positively charged ion. Add one and you get a negative ion. Ions are why salt dissolves and why your nerves can carry signals. Three particles, three charges, and from those the whole chemistry of the universe follows.
pages.cap: Protons and neutrons huddle in the nucleus. Electrons form the outer cloud and do all the chemistry.

pages.h: Count the protons: that is the element
p: What makes gold different from lead? Only one thing: the number of protons in the nucleus. Hydrogen has 1. Helium has 2. Carbon has 6, oxygen 8, iron 26, gold 79, lead 82. Count the protons and you have named the element. That number is called the atomic number.

Change the proton count and you change the element. Medieval alchemists spent centuries trying to turn lead into gold with chemistry. It cannot be done, because chemistry only rearranges electrons. It never touches the nucleus.

Nuclear physics can. In 1980 a team led by the chemist Glenn Seaborg fired particles at bismuth, which has 83 protons, and knocked some out. The result was a few thousand atoms of real gold. The experiment cost far more than the gold was worth, by a factor of about a million million, so no one has repeated it for profit.

The number of electrons in a neutral atom equals the proton count. And since electrons do the chemistry, the proton count secretly controls everything: whether an element is a metal, whether it burns, whether it reacts with water, what colour it is. One number, one element, one personality.
pages.cap: Hop one proton at a time: hydrogen, helium, lithium, beryllium, boron, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen.

pages.h: Isotopes: same element, different weight
p: Protons name the element, but the neutron count can vary. Atoms of one element with different numbers of neutrons are called isotopes. They behave almost identically in chemistry, because they have the same electrons, but they weigh different amounts.

Take carbon. Nearly 99 percent of carbon atoms have 6 protons and 6 neutrons, so they are called carbon-12. About 1 percent have 7 neutrons: carbon-13. And about one atom in a trillion has 8 neutrons: carbon-14. That last one is unstable and slowly breaks down, which makes it a clock for dating old bones and wood. More on that later.

Hydrogen has an isotope with one proton and one neutron called deuterium. It is twice as heavy as ordinary hydrogen. Water made with deuterium is called heavy water, and a litre of it weighs 1.11 kilograms instead of 1.00. About one hydrogen atom in 6,400 on Earth is deuterium, so there is a little heavy water in every glass you drink. Nuclear reactors in Ontario use pure heavy water to help slow down neutrons, and Canada was the world's main maker of it for decades.
pages.cap: Same element on both sides, but one side has extra neutrons and tips the balance.

pages.h: Every atom in your body, except hydrogen, was made inside a star
p: The carbon in your skin, the oxygen in your lungs, the iron in your blood and the calcium in your bones were all forged by nuclear fusion in stars that died before the Sun was born.

pages.q: What decides which element an atom is?
opts: The number of electrons it has gained or lost
pages.why: The proton count is the atomic number. Neutrons make isotopes; gaining or losing electrons makes ions. Neither changes the element.

pages.h: Mendeleev leaves gaps on purpose
p: By 1869 chemists knew 63 elements but had no good way to organize them. A Russian chemist named Dmitri Mendeleev wrote each element on a card with its weight and its habits, and laid the cards out like a game of patience. He noticed that when elements were lined up by weight, their chemical behaviour repeated in a pattern, roughly every eight elements.

Then he did something bold. Where the pattern seemed to demand an element that nobody had found, he left a gap and predicted what the missing element would be like: its weight, its density, the compounds it would form.

In 1875 a French chemist discovered gallium. It matched one of Mendeleev's gaps almost exactly. Scandium followed in 1879 and germanium in 1886, both as predicted. The table stopped being a tidy list and became a map with a legend. A map can tell you what should be somewhere before you go and look.

Mendeleev got some things wrong. He ordered by weight, and a few elements ended up out of place. In 1913 a young English physicist, Henry Moseley, showed that the true order is by proton count. That fixed every one of the misfits.
pages.cap: From one glowing element in a flask to a complete table of 118 took about 350 years.

pages.h: How to read the map
p: Look at a periodic table. The rows are called periods and there are seven of them. Each row tells you how many layers of electrons the atom has. Electrons do not spread evenly. They stack in shells, like layers of an onion, and each shell has a maximum size. The first holds 2 electrons, the second 8, the third 8 at first, then more as you go down.

The columns are called groups. Elements in the same column have the same number of electrons in their outermost shell, and the outermost shell is where chemistry happens. That is why elements in a column behave alike. Lithium, sodium and potassium all have one outer electron, and all of them fizz or explode in water. Helium, neon and argon all have full outer shells, and none of them react with anything.

So the table is a map with two directions. Go across a row and you add one proton and one electron at a time, filling a shell. Go down a column and you keep the same outer electrons but add whole new shells underneath. Once you know an element's address, you can guess its behaviour before you ever open a bottle of it.
pages.cap: Each row of the table adds a new shell of electrons. The outer shell decides how an atom behaves.
pages.fact: Did you know? The table has 118 known elements. About 90 occur naturally on Earth; the rest were made in laboratories.

pages.h: The explosive left edge
p: Drop a piece of sodium into water and it fizzes, races around the surface, and often bursts into yellow flame. Potassium does the same, faster, with a lilac flame. Caesium explodes on contact. These are the alkali metals, the first column of the table, and they are soft enough to cut with a butter knife.

They are so eager to react because each has a single electron in its outer shell, and that lone electron is only loosely held. Atoms are most stable when their outer shell is full. Giving away one electron is the easiest route to that for an alkali metal, so it hands its electron to almost anything nearby, releasing energy as heat and light. Water accepts the electron, releasing hydrogen gas, which then catches fire.

Going down the column, the outer electron sits farther from the nucleus and is held more weakly, so reactions get wilder. Lithium fizzes gently. Caesium shatters the glass. Francium, at the bottom, is so radioactive that there is never more than about 30 grams of it on the whole planet at any moment, so nobody has done the experiment. These metals never exist pure in nature. Every bit of sodium on Earth is locked in salt or rock, waiting.
pages.cap: An alkali metal meets water: the metal gives up an electron, hydrogen gas forms, and the heat sets it alight.
pages.fact: Did you know? Your body needs sodium and potassium ions to send every nerve signal, including the ones you are using to read this.

pages.h: The noble gases: nothing to give
p: On the far right of the table sits a column of elements that refuse to react with anything. Helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon are the noble gases, named for keeping to themselves. Their outer shells are already full, so they have no reason to give, take or share electrons.

That makes them useful. Argon makes up almost 1 percent of the air you breathe, and it is pumped into light bulbs so the hot filament will not burn away. It also protects molten metal during welding. Neon glows orange-red when electricity runs through it, giving us neon signs. Helium is lighter than air and does not burn, which is why it fills party balloons and airships.

Helium has a problem. It is so light that Earth's gravity cannot hold it. Any helium that reaches the top of the atmosphere drifts off into space, forever. The helium we use comes from underground gas fields, where it collects from the slow radioactive decay of uranium in rocks. Hospital MRI scanners need liquid helium at minus 269 degrees Celsius to cool their magnets, and the world's supply is limited. Every helium balloon that floats away takes a little bit of a scarce resource with it.
Chemists argue about whether the heaviest noble gases are truly noble. In 1962 xenon was made to react with fluorine, and now dozens of xenon compounds exist.
pages.cap: A filament bulb is filled with argon. The noble gas will not react with the glowing wire, so the wire lasts for years.

pages.q: Why do sodium and potassium behave so much alike?
opts: They each have one electron in their outer shell
They are both found in sea water
pages.why: Elements in the same column share the same outer-shell electron count, and the outer shell is where chemistry happens.

pages.h: Halogens: one electron short
p: One column to the left of the noble gases sits a family that is just as extreme, in the opposite direction. Fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine each have seven electrons in their outer shell, one short of a full set. They want that last electron badly, and they will take it from almost anything.

Fluorine is the most reactive element known. It attacks glass, sets water on fire, and reacts with nearly every other element, even some noble gases. Chlorine is a green gas that was used as a weapon in the First World War, and in tiny amounts it keeps swimming pools and drinking water free of germs. Iodine is a dark solid that turns purple gas when heated.

Now put the two extremes together. Sodium wants to lose one electron. Chlorine wants to gain one. Mix them and sodium hands its electron to chlorine in a burst of heat and light. The result is sodium chloride: ordinary table salt, a harmless white crystal that you sprinkle on food. Two violent elements make one of the gentlest substances you know. That is the periodic table's best magic trick, and it is just the map doing exactly what the map says.
pages.cap: Salt is sodium ions and chlorine ions locked together. In water the ions let go and drift apart.

pages.h: Metals: a sea of electrons
p: About three quarters of all elements are metals. They fill the whole left and middle of the table. Most are shiny, most conduct electricity and heat, and most can be hammered into sheets or pulled into wires without cracking. Those habits all come from one feature: metal atoms do not hold their outer electrons tightly.

In a lump of metal, the outer electrons leave their atoms and roam freely through the whole piece, like a sea sloshing around fixed islands of positive ions. Apply a voltage and the sea flows: that is an electric current. Heat one end and the fast electrons carry energy to the other end. Hit the metal with a hammer and the ions slide to new positions while the sea simply flows around them, so the metal bends instead of shattering.

Gold shows this best. One gram of gold can be beaten into a sheet half a square metre across and a thousand times thinner than a hair, or drawn into a wire 2 kilometres long. Copper carries the current in nearly every cable in your home because it conducts well and is cheap. Silver conducts even better, but costs about 100 times more. Iron is the most used metal of all. The world makes about 1,900 million tonnes of steel a year, which is mostly iron with a pinch of carbon.
pages.cap: Copper wire carries current because its outer electrons are free to flow through the metal.
pages.fact: Did you know? Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature. Gallium melts in your hand at 30 degrees Celsius.

pages.h: Try it: a periodic table hunt in your kitchen
p: The table is not just in textbooks. You can find at least a dozen elements without leaving the house.
steps: Print or draw a blank periodic table, or use the one in this book's picture as a guide.
Table salt: sodium and chlorine. Baking soda: sodium, hydrogen, carbon, oxygen. Tick them off.
Aluminium foil is pure aluminium. A steel pan is iron with a little carbon and often chromium and nickel. A copper-bottomed pot is copper.
Look at a mineral supplement or cereal box: calcium, iron, zinc, magnesium, potassium, iodine are often listed.
A pencil 'lead' is graphite, pure carbon. Matches contain phosphorus and sulfur. A thermometer or smoke detector may contain mercury or americium, so just read the label, never open them.
Coins: Canadian coins are steel plated with nickel or copper. Colour the elements you found. How many of the 118 did you reach? Most kitchens get 15 to 20.
pages.cap: Canadian coins today are mostly steel, plated with nickel or copper. Three elements in your pocket.
pages.safe: Do not open batteries, thermometers or smoke detectors. Read labels, do not taste or mix anything.

pages.h: Bonds: why atoms stick together
p: Atoms join because joining fills their outer shells. There are three main ways to do it, and the periodic table tells you which one an element will choose.

When a metal meets a non-metal, the metal gives electrons away and the non-metal takes them. The two become oppositely charged ions and stick together by electric attraction. This is an ionic bond. Salt is the classic example. Ionic compounds form hard crystals with high melting points, because every ion is pulled by every neighbour.

When two non-metals meet, neither wants to give up electrons, so they share. Two hydrogen atoms each bring one electron and share the pair, so each feels like it has a full shell of two. This is a covalent bond, and it builds molecules: water, oxygen gas, sugar, every protein in your body.
When metals meet metals, they pool their electrons into the shared sea described earlier. That is a metallic bond.

Breaking bonds costs energy and making bonds releases it. Burning is just swapping weak bonds in fuel and oxygen for strong bonds in carbon dioxide and water, and the leftover energy comes out as heat and light. All of chemistry is atoms trading partners to reach a lower-energy arrangement.
pages.cap: In a water molecule, oxygen shares one pair of electrons with each hydrogen. That is a covalent bond.

pages.h: The strange water molecule
p: Water is two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom, and it is one of the oddest substances in the universe. The oddness comes from its shape. The three atoms are not in a straight line. They form a bent V with an angle of 104.5 degrees, and oxygen pulls the shared electrons toward itself. So the oxygen end is slightly negative and the hydrogen ends are slightly positive.

That tiny imbalance means water molecules grab each other, positive end to negative end, in what chemists call hydrogen bonds. Each one is weak, but there are billions of billions of them in every drop, and together they change everything.

Because the molecules cling, water needs a lot of heat to warm up or boil. A kilogram of water takes 4,184 joules to warm by one degree, more than almost any other common liquid. That is why oceans keep coastal cities mild and why your body can use sweat to cool down.

When water freezes, the hydrogen bonds lock the molecules into an open hexagonal lattice with more empty space than the liquid had. So ice is about 9 percent less dense than water and floats. Nearly every other substance sinks when it freezes. If ice sank, lakes would freeze from the bottom up and life in cold climates might never have survived.
pages.cap: In ice, water molecules lock into a hexagonal lattice with gaps in it. That is why ice floats.
pages.fact: Did you know? Water is the only common substance found naturally as solid, liquid and gas at Earth's surface temperatures.

pages.h: Why gold is gold
p: Most metals are silvery. Iron, aluminium, silver, nickel, tin, zinc: all grey-white. Gold is yellow and copper is reddish, and the reason is one of the strangest in chemistry.

White light is a mix of all colours. A metal looks silvery because its free electrons reflect every colour about equally. Gold's electrons are different. Gold has 79 protons, and the inner electrons of such a heavy atom are pulled so strongly that they move at more than half the speed of light. Einstein's rules say fast things get heavier, and these heavier electrons sit in slightly tighter orbits. That shifts the energy gold's electrons need to jump, just enough that gold absorbs blue light and reflects the rest. Take blue out of white and you get yellow.

Without relativity, gold would be silvery, and mercury would probably be a solid at room temperature instead of a liquid. Copper is reddish for a different reason: its electrons happen to absorb blue and green light even without relativity's help.

Gold's heavy, tightly held electrons also make it lazy. It does not rust, tarnish or react with water or air, which is why gold coins buried for 2,000 years come up shining, while iron swords turn to rust. The same relativistic effect that paints gold yellow also makes it last forever.
pages.cap: White light holds every colour. Gold absorbs the blue and reflects the rest, so the metal looks yellow.

pages.q: Why does ice float on water?
opts: Ice has air bubbles trapped in it
Frozen water molecules lock into an open lattice that takes up more space
pages.why: Hydrogen bonds hold ice molecules in a hexagonal pattern with gaps, so ice is about 9 percent less dense than liquid water.

pages.h: The Big Bang made only three elements
p: Go back 13.8 billion years. The universe is a few minutes old and hotter than the centre of the Sun. It is a soup of protons, neutrons and electrons, with no atoms at all. As it expands and cools, protons and neutrons start sticking together. For about 20 minutes, the whole universe is a fusion reactor.

Then it is over. The universe has cooled and spread out too much for fusion to continue. What it made, by mass, is about 75 percent hydrogen, 25 percent helium, and a trace of lithium. That is it. Three elements. No carbon, no oxygen, no iron. Nothing to make rocks, water, or people.

Those first atoms could not even form properly for another 380,000 years, because it was too hot for electrons to settle around nuclei. When they finally did, the universe became transparent for the first time, and the light released then is still arriving today as a faint microwave glow from every direction.

Then nothing much happened for a hundred million years. The universe was dark, made of only hydrogen and helium, waiting. Every other element on the table, the other 115 or so, had to be made later, somewhere else. That somewhere is the subject of the next three chapters.
pages.cap: In its first 20 minutes the universe fused hydrogen into helium and then stopped. Everything heavier came later.

pages.h: Stars are element factories
p: Gravity gathered the first hydrogen into clumps and squeezed them until their centres reached about 10 million degrees. At that temperature hydrogen nuclei slam together hard enough to overcome their electric repulsion and fuse into helium. The fusion releases energy, the energy holds the star up against gravity, and the star shines. That is what a star is: a slow fusion fire balanced against its own weight.

The Sun converts about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium every second. The helium weighs slightly less than the hydrogen that made it, and the missing 4 million tonnes a second becomes the sunlight that warms Earth. The Sun has been doing this for 4.6 billion years and has fuel for about 5 billion more.

When the hydrogen in a star's core runs low, the core shrinks, heats up, and starts fusing helium into carbon, and some carbon into oxygen. In a star like the Sun that is where it ends. But stars more than about eight times the Sun's mass go further. Carbon fuses to neon, neon to oxygen, oxygen to silicon, silicon to iron. Each step runs hotter and faster. The last step, silicon to iron, takes about a day. The star's inside looks like an onion, with iron at the centre and lighter elements in shells around it.
pages.cap: A star balances fusion pushing out against gravity pulling in. The balance can last billions of years.

pages.h: Iron is the wall. Supernovas break through.
p: Fusion makes energy because joining light nuclei gives a nucleus that is more tightly bound, and the extra binding energy escapes. But the tightness peaks at iron. Fusing iron into anything heavier takes energy in rather than giving it out. So when a giant star's core turns to iron, the fire goes out.

Without fusion pushing outward, gravity wins instantly. The iron core, about the mass of the Sun, collapses from the size of Earth to the size of a city in less than a second. The collapse slams to a halt when the core becomes as dense as an atomic nucleus, and the rebound, plus a flood of ghostly particles called neutrinos, blasts the rest of the star into space. This is a supernova, and for weeks it can outshine its whole galaxy.

In that blast, nuclei are bombarded with so many neutrons so quickly that they build up past iron: zinc, copper, silver, tin, and more. The explosion then flings these new elements across light years, where they mix into gas clouds that later form new stars and planets. The Sun is a third-generation star, built from the debris of earlier ones. The iron in your blood took that route: forged in a core, scattered by an explosion, gathered by gravity.
Astronomers watched one up close in 1987, in a nearby galaxy, and caught its neutrinos three hours before the light arrived.
pages.cap: A massive star dies in a supernova, scattering new elements into space for the next generation of stars.

pages.h: Gold comes from colliding dead stars
p: For decades textbooks said supernovas made all the heavy elements. Then the numbers refused to add up. Supernovas did not seem able to make nearly enough gold, platinum and uranium to explain what we find on Earth. Something else had to be forging the heaviest elements.

The answer came on 17 August 2017. Gravitational-wave detectors felt two neutron stars, the collapsed cores of dead giant stars, spiralling into each other 130 million light years away. Seventy observatories swung to look. They saw a glow that faded over days from blue to red, exactly the signature predicted for a cloud of freshly made heavy elements, hot with their own radioactivity. Astronomers call it a kilonova.

Neutron stars are almost pure neutrons, and when two of them smash together they spray out neutron-rich debris that captures neutrons faster than anything else in the universe. In that debris, nuclei climb straight up the table to gold, platinum and beyond. That single collision made an estimated 10 or more Earth masses of gold, though estimates vary a lot.

Scientists still argue about the share. Some think rare, fast-spinning supernovas also contribute heavy elements, especially in the early universe. But the gold in a ring almost certainly spent its first moments in the wreckage of two dead stars, long before the Sun existed.
pages.cap: Two neutron stars collide. The debris is so rich in neutrons that it forges gold, platinum and uranium in seconds.

pages.h: The calcium in your bones was made in a star that died before the Sun was born
p: An adult body holds about 1 kilogram of calcium, nearly all of it in bones and teeth. Every gram of it was fused inside a dying giant star, blown into space, and gathered by gravity into the cloud that became the Sun, Earth and you.

pages.h: Radioactivity: atoms that fall apart
p: In 1896 a French physicist named Henri Becquerel left some uranium salt on a wrapped photographic plate in a drawer. When he developed the plate it was fogged, as if light had reached it through the paper. It had not. The uranium itself was giving off invisible rays. Marie Curie named the effect radioactivity and spent her life studying it, discovering two new elements, polonium and radium, along the way.

Here is what is going on. Some nuclei have an unstable mix of protons and neutrons. Sooner or later they rearrange, spitting out a piece and turning into a different element. There are three main kinds of piece. An alpha particle is two protons and two neutrons, stopped by a sheet of paper. A beta particle is a fast electron, stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium. A gamma ray is a burst of very high energy light, which takes thick lead or concrete to block.

Radioactivity is not rare or unnatural. It warms Earth's interior, drives volcanoes and continental drift, and happens inside your own body about 5,000 times a second, mostly from potassium-40 and carbon-14. In large doses it damages the molecules in cells, which is why it is both dangerous and, carefully aimed, a tool for killing cancer. The dose is what matters, not the mere presence.
pages.cap: An unstable nucleus throws out a piece of itself and becomes a different element. That is radioactive decay.
pages.fact: Did you know? Marie Curie's notebooks are still radioactive and are kept in lead-lined boxes. Readers must sign a waiver to see them.

pages.h: Half-lives: the clock inside the rock
p: You cannot say when one particular radioactive atom will decay. But with a large number of atoms, you can say exactly how long it takes for half of them to go. That time is the half-life, and it is different for every isotope. Polonium-214 has a half-life of 0.00016 seconds. Carbon-14: 5,730 years. Uranium-238: 4.5 billion years, about the age of Earth.

That steadiness makes radioactive atoms into clocks. Carbon-14 forms constantly in the upper air and gets into every living thing through food. When a plant or animal dies, the intake stops and the carbon-14 starts to tick away. Measure how much is left and you know how long ago the thing died, back to about 50,000 years. This is how archaeologists date wooden tools, bones and ancient fabric.

For rocks, scientists use slower clocks. Uranium-238 decays through a chain of steps into lead-206. Compare the uranium and lead in a crystal and you can date it to a few million years, even if it is billions of years old. This is how we know Earth formed 4.54 billion years ago, and how the oldest known crystals, zircons from Western Australia, were dated to 4.4 billion years. The periodic table turns out to contain a set of stopwatches, each running at its own speed, that started when the rocks first cooled.
pages.cap: Each rock layer formed on top of the one below. Radioactive clocks in the layers tell you exactly how long ago.

pages.h: Bananas are radioactive, and so are you
p: Potassium is an essential element. Your nerves and muscles cannot work without it, and a banana contains about 400 milligrams. One potassium atom in 8,500 is potassium-40, which is radioactive. So every banana gives off a tiny amount of radiation, and so does every person, every potato, and every brick.

The scale matters. Scientists measure radiation dose in sieverts. Eating one banana gives about 0.1 microsieverts, a tenth of a millionth of a sievert. A dental X-ray is about 5 microsieverts. A return flight from Toronto to Vancouver, where the thin air blocks fewer cosmic rays, is roughly 40. A chest CT scan is about 7,000. The average Canadian receives about 1,800 microsieverts a year from natural sources alone, without a single medical scan.

The biggest natural source is radon, a noble gas made when uranium in rocks and soil decays. It seeps into basements and is the second leading cause of lung cancer after smoking. Testing a home for radon is cheap, and Health Canada recommends it.

Your body cannot tell where radiation comes from; a sievert is a sievert. What it can do, remarkably well, is repair damage from the small, steady doses life has always delivered. Life evolved on a radioactive planet and has had four billion years of practice.

v.title: Where your yearly radiation comes from (%)

pages.cap: Roughly where an average person's radiation dose comes from. Radon from the ground is the biggest share.

pages.q: Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5,730 years. A bone has one quarter of the carbon-14 of a living animal. How old is it?
pages.why: After one half-life, half remains. After two half-lives, a quarter remains. Two times 5,730 is 11,460 years.

pages.h: Making elements that nature never made
p: Uranium, with 92 protons, is the heaviest element found in any quantity on Earth. Everything past it on the table was made by people. Starting in 1940, scientists built heavier and heavier nuclei by firing one nucleus at another in a particle accelerator and hoping, very occasionally, that they would stick.

It gets harder with every step. Element 118, oganesson, was made at a laboratory in Dubna, Russia, between 2002 and 2005. In total about five atoms were detected, and each one lasted less than a thousandth of a second before falling apart. Oganesson is named after Yuri Oganessian, one of the few people to have an element named after them while still alive. The last four elements, 113 to 118, received their names in 2016. Element 113 was made in Japan and is called nihonium, the first element discovered in Asia.
The chase continues. Teams in Japan, Russia, Germany and the United States are hunting for element 119, which would start a brand new row of the table. So far, no one has found it.

Why bother, if the atoms vanish in a blink? Theory predicts an 'island of stability', a combination of protons and neutrons where superheavy atoms might last minutes, years, or longer. Nobody knows if the island exists or where it is. Scientists argue about whether the table even has an end, or simply fades out.
pages.cap: To make a new element, scientists fuse two nuclei. The result may exist for less than a millisecond.

pages.h: Try it: grow a salt crystal
p: Sodium and chloride ions arrange themselves in a perfect cube pattern. Give them a few days and you can see it with your own eyes.
steps: Warm about 250 millilitres of water in a mug until it is hot but not boiling. Ask an adult if you are using a stove.
Stir in table salt a spoonful at a time until no more will dissolve and a little sits on the bottom. This is a saturated solution.
Pour the clear liquid, not the undissolved salt, into a clean glass jar.
Tie a short piece of cotton string or a clean paper clip to a pencil and lay the pencil across the jar so the string hangs into the liquid.
Put the jar somewhere still and warm, loosely covered with paper. Check every day. As water evaporates, ions lock onto the string in cube shapes.
After a week, look at the crystals with a magnifying glass. Every one should have square faces, because that is the only shape sodium and chloride ions can pack into.
pages.cap: Salt dissolves into separate ions. As the water leaves, the ions snap back into cube-shaped crystals.
pages.safe: Use oven mitts for hot water. Do not eat the crystals once they have sat out.

pages.h: The chemistry of life uses six elements
p: Out of 118 elements, life is built almost entirely from six: carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus and sulfur. Chemists call them CHNOPS. By mass, you are about 65 percent oxygen, 18 percent carbon, 10 percent hydrogen and 3 percent nitrogen, mostly because you are mostly water. Those six together make up about 97 percent of you. Calcium and potassium, plus small amounts of about 20 others, make the rest.

Each has a job. Carbon builds the frames of every molecule in a cell. Hydrogen and oxygen make water, the liquid everything else floats in. Nitrogen sits in every protein and in the letters of DNA. Phosphorus forms the backbone of DNA and is at the heart of ATP, the molecule that carries energy around inside cells. Sulfur pins proteins into their folded shapes.

Why these six? They are all common in the universe, all light, and all able to form strong, stable bonds with carbon and with each other. Oxygen and sulfur sit in the same column of the table, and so do nitrogen and phosphorus. The table's map explains why life could swap between them.

Trace elements matter too. Iron in your blood carries oxygen. Iodine in your thyroid sets your metabolism. A diet with no cobalt, which sits at the centre of vitamin B12, would eventually make a person very ill. Life uses the whole map, just unevenly.
pages.cap: A single cell is a bag of water full of carbon-based molecules, with phosphorus holding the DNA together.

pages.h: Carbon: the element that builds
p: Carbon has four electrons in its outer shell and needs four more to fill it. So each carbon atom can make four strong bonds, in any direction, with other carbons or with almost anything else. No other element does this so well. Silicon, directly below carbon on the table, also makes four bonds, but they are weaker and it cannot build long stable chains in water.

Four bonds means carbon can build chains, branches, rings, sheets and cages, and there is no limit to the size. A single molecule of DNA from one of your chromosomes contains billions of carbon atoms in one unbroken structure. Chemists have identified tens of millions of different carbon compounds, far more than for all other elements combined.

Even pure carbon shows off. Arrange the atoms in a rigid 3D lattice with every atom bonded to four others and you get diamond, the hardest natural substance. Arrange them in flat sheets with three bonds each and you get graphite, the soft grey stuff in a pencil, where sheets slide off onto the paper. Peel off a single sheet, one atom thick, and you have graphene, first isolated in 2004 with sticky tape. It is 200 times stronger than steel for its weight and conducts electricity better than copper. Same element, three personalities, decided purely by how the bonds are arranged.
pages.cap: The twisted ladder of DNA is a carbon frame. Four bonds per atom let carbon build molecules of any size.

pages.h: Every helium balloon you let go leaves the planet for good
p: Helium is so light that Earth's gravity cannot keep it. It rises to the top of the atmosphere and drifts into space. Earth's helium is made only by slow radioactive decay underground, and we are using it far faster than rocks can make it.

pages.h: Elements that are running low
p: Elements do not get used up in the way fuel does. An atom of copper in a thrown-away phone is still copper. But it can be scattered so thinly that collecting it costs more than digging up fresh ore. Several elements are now in that uncomfortable zone.

Helium is the clearest case. It escapes to space, cannot be made in useful amounts, and is needed for MRI scanners, rocket fuel systems and making computer chips. Phosphorus is another. Every farm on Earth depends on phosphate fertilizer, and about 70 percent of the world's known reserves sit in one country, Morocco. Scientists argue about whether supplies will tighten in 50 years or 300, but nobody argues that it is infinite.

Then there are the rare earth metals, 17 elements with names like neodymium and dysprosium, used in the magnets inside electric motors, wind turbines and headphones. They are not actually rare, but they are hard to separate from each other, and one country, China, does roughly 90 percent of the world's refining.

The answer is the same for all of them: recycle. A tonne of old phones contains about 300 grams of gold, roughly 100 times more than a tonne of typical gold ore. Chemistry can take the elements back out. Whether we bother is a decision, not a law of nature.
pages.cap: A city is a mine in reverse. The elements in its wires, batteries and phones can be recovered, if someone chooses to.
pages.fact: Did you know? About 60 of the 118 elements are inside a modern smartphone.

pages.h: What we still do not know about atoms
p: The periodic table looks finished. It is not. Here are some of the open questions.

Where does the table end? Nobody knows if element 119 or 120 can be made, or whether a stable island of superheavy elements exists. Theory suggests that above about 173 protons, the electric field of the nucleus would become so strong that electrons could no longer behave normally, and the whole idea of a chemical element might break down. That is a prediction, not an observation.

Do the heaviest elements follow the map? Oganesson sits under the noble gases, so it should be an unreactive gas. Calculations say its electrons move so fast that relativity scrambles its behaviour, and it may be a reactive solid instead. With only five atoms ever made, no one has checked.

How big is a proton? In 2010 a new measurement found the proton 4 percent smaller than everyone thought. It took a decade of careful work to mostly settle the disagreement, and a few labs are still checking.

Why these elements? The strengths of the forces inside the nucleus are just right for carbon and oxygen to form in stars. Change them slightly and there would be no chemistry of life. Whether that is luck, necessity or something else is a question that physicists argue about and cannot yet answer.
Every blank on this map is waiting for someone.
pages.cap: The map has edges nobody has reached. Past element 118, and inside the proton, the territory is unexplored.

qs: Mendeleev predicted elements before anyone found them. What would it take to trust a prediction like that? What if gallium had not matched?
Every atom in your body has been part of other things: stars, rocks, dinosaurs, other people. Does that change what 'you' means?
Helium escapes Earth forever once released. Should party balloons be allowed? Who gets to decide how a scarce element is used?
